item.title: Adequate Water Consumption May Enhance Psychological Health
item.description:
Cognition

Adequate Water Consumption May Enhance Psychological Health

Could better cognition and emotional regulation be a sip away?

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Water helps produce neurotransmitters, making adequate hydration essential for optimal psychological health.
  • Adequate water intake is correlated to better cognitive performance and a decrease in depression and anxiety.
  • Too much water, however, can dilute sodium and potassium levels and cause neuropsychiatric complications.
Source: ELG21/Pixabay

We always hear it’s important to stay hydrated, but aside from the obvious, like flushing out toxins and not feeling like a raisin, have you ever wondered why water is so important to our health?

It seems that nowadays drinking water has become trendy, or at least the water containers have, leading to inadvertently well-hydrated otherwise hydrophobic citizens. Given humans are about 60% water, it makes sense that staying alive requires adequate hydration. But that’s the big picture.

The physiological functions (e.g. Popkin et al., 2011) of water range from thermoregulation, such as sweating to digestion, such as preventing constipation; kidney function, where water is required to filter waste from the bloodstream into urine; and it is essential for neurotransmitter production (e.g., Mustafayeva, 2025) and synaptic communication in the brain.

How hydration benefits brain health

The last item is closely linked to psychological functioning, as neurotransmitters (e.g., Sheffler et al., 2023) are involved in mood, sleep, cognition, appetite, and motivation. Good hydration, therefore, is essential to mental health. Also, just being near water has positive psychological effects, but more on that later.

While some people can be so dehydrated they became delirious or develop significant cognitive impairments, most people experience more benign, but nonetheless performance-impairing effects of dehydration at times. In fact, researchers Trinies et al. (2016) tell us that there is a well-established link between hydration and improved cognitive performance. For example, exercise-induced dehydration has been shown to negatively impact memory, attention and visuospatial function. Also, children who drank more water have been recorded as performing better on tests of memory and attention (e.g. Edmonds, 2012).

Other researchers such as Haghighatdoost et al. (2018) found that lower daily water intake has been associated with increased risk of depression and anxiety. This was backed by an earlier study by Pross et al. (2014) who reported that when people who drank high volumes of water decreased their intake, they reported feeling less calm, content and vigorous, and a decrease in positive emotions. The reverse was found in people who increased their water consumption.

One hypothesis as to the water-mood link is that dehydration increases the stress hormone cortisol. Kashi et al. (2025) noted that people who drank less than 1.2 liters of water per day had higher serum cortisol levels than people who drank 2-4 liters. An increase in cortisol can contribute to irritability, anger, appetite and sleep disturbances. Hence, one may feel moody if they become dehydrated, like one might feel “hangry” when they have not eaten for some time.

How much water is optimal?

This of course will vary, but it’s recommended that, in general, adult females consume 2.7 liters and adult males 3.7 liters of water per day (e.g. Seal et al., 2022; Faizan & Rouster, 2023). I’ve heard a lot of people say they don’t meet that requirement because, “I’m not thirsty,” but that’s hollow logic. When you’re thirsty, you’re already dehydrated. Further, maybe you do drink a lot of water, but nonetheless still feel thirsty, and thus are dehydrated. The culprits can range from underlying medical conditions like diabetes to excess caffeine consumption and medication side effects.

The take-home is that dehydration is a physical and psychological stressor. If you’re not a water drinker and experience brain fog, fatigue, moodiness, and/or anxiety, the remedy might be a trendy water bottle away. For those prone to anxiety and mood-related disorders who don’t prioritize water consumption, dehydration could be exacerbating your symptoms.

On the flip side, there is such a thing as drinking too much water. According to the National Kidney Foundation (2023), this can lead to dangerously diluted sodium and potassium levels, called hypernatremia. It is sometimes referred to as “water intoxication”. Hypernatremia can cause anything from headaches to neuropsychiatric conditions. When I worked in a jail, there was an inmate who drank an inordinate amount of water for some reason. When I met with him, he was so disorganized that he was speaking “word salad” and physically uncoordinated.

Source: 99mimimi/Pixabay

Of course, checking with your doctor about increasing water intake is a good idea, as it could negatively affect some medical conditions like edema.

Look at the water, lower your stress?

Speaking of water’s role in stress reduction, it’s not only by consumption. While it is well-documented that being in nature has significant stress-reducing effects (e.g. Stott et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025), researchers have been finding that merely looking at water has salutary effects. For example, researchers Coss and Keller (2022) reported that average blood pressure and heart rate decreased and relaxation increased when subjects were looking at water.

For those interested in a deeper understanding of how and why being near or in the water makes you feel good, marine biologist Wallace Nichols wrote: Blue Mind: The Surprising Science That Shows How Being Near, In, On, or Under Water Can Make You Happier, Healthier, More Connected, and Better at What You Do.

The information should not replace personalized care or intervention from an individual’s provider or formal supervision if you’re a practitioner or student.

item.title: Differentiating DID, C-PTSD, and Dissociation
item.description:
Dissociation

Differentiating DID, C-PTSD, and Dissociation

Specialized assessment matters when trauma and dissociation overlap.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Dissociation can occur in C-PTSD, DID, and other conditions.
  • C-PTSD and DID can overlap, but they are not the same diagnosis.
  • DID involves disruptions in identity and memory that go beyond ordinary forgetting.
  • Specialized trauma training helps clinicians make sense of overlapping symptoms.
Dissociative experiences can be deeply distressing, even when they are difficult for others to recognize.
Source: Ground Picture/Shutterstock

In today’s information-rich environment, clinicians and the general public alike are increasingly familiar with terms such as dissociation, switching, parts, and complex PTSD. This has helped many people put words to difficult experiences, but it can also make related concepts seem interchangeable when they are not.

C-PTSD, dissociative identity disorder (DID), and dissociation are closely connected, but distinguishing among them is essential for accurate diagnosis and appropriate care planning. Doing so requires careful attention to patterns involving memory, identity, agency, and relationships over time.

Why Dissociation Can Be Difficult to Interpret

People with trauma-related symptoms may shut down, feel far away from themselves, lose track of parts of an experience, or feel divided inside. Dissociation can disrupt awareness, memory, identity, emotion, perception, and connection to the body (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). Someone may move through the day on “autopilot” or later struggle to remember conversations or stretches of time.

Because these experiences can occur in C-PTSD, DID, and other conditions, their presence alone does not establish a diagnosis. The same symptom can mean different things depending on its frequency, triggers, severity, and effect on daily life.

How Dissociation Can Appear in C-PTSD

C-PTSD is recognized as a distinct diagnosis in the World Health Organization’s ICD-11. Along with the core symptoms of PTSD, it involves ongoing difficulties with emotion regulation, self-concept, and relationships (World Health Organization, 2024).

For some people, prolonged or repeated trauma can lead to emotional shutdown, detachment from oneself, a sense that the world is unreal, or fragmented memories. These responses may intensify when escape or reliable support is unavailable. Others experience C-PTSD through hypervigilance, shame, avoidance, and difficulty feeling safe with others. Dissociation can be part of C-PTSD, but it is not required for diagnosis because it is not present in every case (Hyland et al., 2024; World Health Organization, 2024).

What Distinguishes DID

DID involves identity disruption and recurrent memory gaps beyond ordinary forgetting. These disruptions can affect a person’s sense of self and agency, behavior, emotions, perceptions, and access to personal memories (American Psychiatric Association, 2022).

DID often presents more subtly than popular portrayals suggest. Someone may find messages they do not remember sending or realize that periods of time are missing. They may also hear internal voices or notice abrupt changes in perspective, preferences, skills, or sense of age (Dorahy et al., 2014).

Many people with DID first seek treatment for depression, anxiety, sleep problems, or relationship difficulties. If they minimize or do not recognize their dissociative experiences, the underlying pattern may be missed (Loewenstein & Brand, 2023).

Diagnosis should rest on current symptoms and patterns of functioning, without pressure to recover memories or tell a particular story.

Where C-PTSD and DID Overlap

Both conditions can involve shame, difficulty regulating emotions, relationship problems, dissociation, and a sense that different “parts” come forward in different situations. In C-PTSD, persistent shame and a harsh inner critic can become an especially painful part of the pattern.

Parts language alone does not indicate DID. Many people recognize frightened, angry, or capable parts while maintaining continuous identity and memory.

A person with C-PTSD may shift sharply between emotional states while still recognizing each as part of themselves. In DID, shifts usually involve deeper disruptions in memory, identity, and the sense of who is directing thoughts or actions.

Why Diagnosis Can Be Difficult

Internal voices may be interpreted as psychosis, abrupt changes in behavior as mood episodes, and gaps in memory as stress or inattention. Similar overlap can occur with borderline personality disorder, bipolar disorder, substance-related conditions, sleep disorders, neurological conditions, and attention difficulties (Dorahy et al., 2014; Loewenstein & Brand, 2023).

Accurate diagnosis requires examining when symptoms began, what triggers them, how memory and identity are affected, medical and substance-use history, and responses to previous treatment.

A careful assessment considers patterns in memory, identity, agency, and daily functioning over time.
Source: Prostock-Studio/istock

What a Careful Assessment Looks Like

A careful assessment unfolds over time. The clinician may begin by asking about moments of detachment or unreality, then explore gaps in memory and changes in the person’s sense of self or control. These questions should be direct but neutral so the pattern can emerge without steering the person toward a particular explanation.

Screening tools can help identify areas that need closer attention, but they are only one part of the process. No questionnaire score can diagnose DID on its own (Carlson et al., 1993; Mychailyszyn et al., 2021).

The clinician must then consider how these experiences affect daily life, whether they follow a consistent pattern, and whether another diagnosis offers a better explanation. Cultural context is also essential. Experiences involving trance, identity, or possession may carry different meanings across cultures and should be explored carefully rather than automatically treated as signs of a disorder.

Why Specialized Trauma Training Matters

Many clinicians receive limited training in complex trauma and dissociation. Without that expertise, DID may be missed or dissociative symptoms interpreted through another diagnostic lens.

The reverse is also possible. Trauma history, parts language, or a high screening score does not automatically mean DID. Specialized training helps clinicians ask neutral questions and pace treatment appropriately.

When significant dissociation is present, treatment often begins with safety, stabilization, grounding, emotion regulation, and daily functioning. Trauma processing may come later, once the person can remain more oriented during difficult material (International Society for the Study of Trauma and Dissociation, 2011).

Accurate Diagnosis Can Guide Healing

Online information can help people recognize that lost time, emotional detachment, internal conflict, or feeling unreal deserves attention. It cannot determine what those experiences mean for a particular person.

Accurate diagnosis is about understanding someone’s experience well enough to guide appropriate care. When trauma and dissociation overlap, specialized knowledge, careful listening, and thoughtful pacing can create a safer path toward stability and a fuller life.

item.title: There Is No “Attention Deficit” in Attention-Deficit Disorder
item.description:
ADHD

There Is No “Attention Deficit” in Attention-Deficit Disorder

What parents get wrong about attention-deficit disorder.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • ADD’s name is misleading—it implies a total lack of attention rather than a dysregulation of attention.
  • People with ADD can hyperfocus intensely on some tasks, showing ability to focus, although poorly regulated.
  • Reframing ADD as dysregulation (not deficit) reduces stigma, shame, and delayed diagnosis.
ADD doesn't always mean difficulty focusing.
Source: Vika Glitter / Pexels

Attention-deficit disorder (ADD) has an extremely misleading name. Actually, it’s beyond misleading. It’s flat out wrong. This inaccuracy causes a lot of misconceptions socially and confusion among patients and families. It’s time for a change.

I’ve had family after family come into therapy with a child experiencing attention problems and say something to the effect of, “If Johnny can choose to focus on video games, he can choose to focus on his homework. So he must not have ADD. He’s just not trying hard enough.” This is an understandable but deeply flawed conclusion about how ADD works. After discussing this thought process in detail with many parents, I think the problem is rooted in the name.

To understand the issue, first let’s start with a similar example that most people are familiar with where a misleading name caused a public education catastrophe. In the late 20th century, when scientists first understood that the Earth’s average temperatures were rising, to help explain their observations to the public, they coined the term “global warming” (Broecker, 1975). If you haven’t heard this phrase in a while, there’s a reason: It not only failed to increase public understanding of the phenomenon but actually accomplished the exact opposite of this goal, leading to confusion and denial, a fallout we are still dealing with today.

The problem was that rising overall temperatures cause all sorts of instances of extreme weather fluctuations, including periods of intense cold in winter months. Whenever someone would experience such a frigid climate, this would cause cognitive dissonance with the idea of a global “warming.” It was not uncommon to hear people say things along the lines of, “This is the coldest I’ve ever felt. How could the globe possibly be warming?” The word “warming” was critically problematic, so over time, “climate change” slowly replaced global warming as a term that more effectively conveys the idea of what’s happening (NASA, n.d.).

So where does the term attention-deficit disorder fall short? If you know anyone with ADD, you know they can often hyperfocus on certain things (Ashinoff & Abu-Akel, 2021). A child who can’t focus on homework for 30 seconds may be able to play video games for hours without even realizing how much time has gone by. This type of hyperfocus on some tasks is a common experience of people with ADD. It can lead to “time blindness,” in which they’ve been focusing so intently on one thing that the outside world melted away (Marx et al., 2022). Clearly then, people who have ADD have the capacity to sustain attention under certain circumstances, so what’s going on?

A Dysregulation of Attention

At its heart, ADD is not a deficit of attention but a dysregulation of attention (Cortese et al., 2025). People with ADD may not be paying attention to the task that they and the people around them want them to be paying attention to, but they are paying attention to something. That something may shift rapidly, or be sustained for hours, but the ability to focus is present. It’s just not well regulated.

Why is this distinction important? People with ADD and their loved ones need to know that ADD does not render a person incapable of focusing. The fundamental neurological infrastructure required to focus is already in place. In many cases, techniques such as mindfulness exercises can help the person enhance these focusing skills (Oliva et al., 2021). But even if not, the shift from viewing their neurodivergence as a deficit to a difference may be empowering.

To be clear, I am not saying that a person can choose to avoid their ADD symptoms, nor am I denying the importance of medication for many patients in helping mitigate them. Patients’ struggles are real and often beyond their control to adequately address.

My goal here is actually the opposite: to help emphasize the fact that just because someone with ADD can focus on some things, that does not mean they are choosing to neglect the others.

So when families come in saying that their child must not have an attention deficit because he can pay attention to video games, I explain the difference between a deficit and dysregulation, and this often, after some time, can help the parent understand.

While a therapist can explain this to families once they come to treatment, the problem is that many children won’t even make it to an appointment because many parents and teachers see these instances of hyperfocus and assume the child must not have ADD.

In my experience, this misconception that ADD means total inability to focus is a widespread problem. I’ve had many young adult clients in college or the later years of high school find out they have ADD, and when I ask the families why it wasn’t identified earlier, they say it never crossed their mind because the child was able to focus on some things. ADD seems particularly prone to fly under the radar if the child doesn’t have the hyperactivity component that can sometimes be present. If they weren’t causing a “problem” in school, the time and resources were not spent to investigate and identify what they were experiencing.

Although not directly related to this naming issue, I want to mention another misconception. I often see cases where, as a young adult, a client becomes aware of their attention challenges (even if they only vaguely recognize them as something “wrong” in their mind) and they feel so ashamed that they build an elaborate mental world of denial and fantasies of success. For example, a child who felt pressure to attend an Ivy League college may tell her whole family she was accepted to one, and even keep up that ruse until outside factors expose it as false.

In these cases, parents feel the child is intentionally lying and betraying their trust. While I don’t completely discount some element of choice, I think it explains much more to view this situation not as manipulation but as an escape into a fantasy world that denies the truth even to themselves. After all, people who deny climate change are not sitting there consciously thinking, “I’m lying to myself and everyone around me.” They are simply blocking out a truth that is so unpleasant for them that they’ve deceived even themselves.

Some Progress on Understanding Mental Health Disorders

Although there is a long way to go, society has made some progress on understanding mental health disorders. With depression, for example, there are still misconceptions. For example, a family member may still ask questions like, “What’s going on in your life that’s causing you to be depressed?” (There often is no “why.” It can be purely physiological [American Psychiatric Association, n.d.]).

But, on the other hand, people generally seem to have a better understanding regarding some other aspects of depression. For example, I’ve noticed a trend lately, supported by research, toward improvement in family members’ understanding that postpartum depression is real and not the mother’s fault (although again, this is not universal and there’s still much progress to be made [Khadka et al., 2024]).

We need to make similar progress on ADD. Social awareness can slowly increase to the point that some of its nuances transform into common knowledge. The more that we discuss ADD openly and turn away from stigma, the sooner we can reach such a point of understanding. If you have questions about ADD, reach out to a therapist and talk about them.

item.title: When Depression Enters the Courtroom
item.description:
Forensic Psychology

When Depression Enters the Courtroom

Untangling forensic depression.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Sometimes depression changes how people respond to conflict, and it may lead to legal trouble.
  • What if depression affects more than mood? It may contribute to behaviors that end in courtrooms.
  • Under certain conditions, depression may amplify the path toward aggression, conflict, and legal consequences.

Most people think of depression as an illness of withdrawal. A person loses energy. Stops answering the phone. Misses work. Sleeps too much, or too little. Life shrinks. In our cultural imagination, depression hurts primarily the person who suffers from it.

That image is true. But it is not the whole truth.

Over the past several years, researchers have begun examining a possibility that few clinicians—and even fewer members of the public—have considered: under some circumstances, depression may increase the risk of behaviors that eventually bring people into contact with the legal system.

I call this possibility forensic depression.

This phrase does not imply that depressed people are criminals; far from it. The overwhelming majority of people living with depression are never violent, never arrested, and never commit serious offenses. They are much more likely to suffer harm than to inflict it.

The question is subtler. Could depression become one ingredient in a chain of events that ends in aggression, domestic violence, reckless behavior, or other acts with legal consequences? Surprisingly, the answer may sometimes be yes.

That possibility initially seems counterintuitive. Depression appears passive; crime appears active. Yet clinical reality is often less tidy.

Depression is not simply sadness. It frequently includes irritability, agitation, hopelessness, emotional pain, impaired judgment, poor impulse regulation, disturbed sleep, and profound social isolation. Some depressed individuals become emotionally numb. Others become explosively reactive. When these processes unfold alongside alcohol misuse, chronic stress, humiliation, financial collapse, relationship conflict, or longstanding personality vulnerabilities, the resulting behavior can differ dramatically from the stereotype of the quiet, withdrawn patient.

The important point is that depression rarely acts alone.

Think of it less as a cause than as an amplifier. Just as high blood pressure does not inevitably produce a heart attack but substantially raises risk when combined with other factors, depression may magnify the likelihood that already strained situations end badly.

The scientific evidence is still developing. Prospective longitudinal studies have reported that depression predicts later aggressive or delinquent behavior in some populations, although other equally rigorous studies have failed to find such associations. The jury—scientifically speaking—is still out.

This uncertainty is precisely why the topic deserves attention. Science advances by asking uncomfortable questions before definitive answers are available. Perhaps the more interesting question is why depression might contribute to forensic outcomes. One possibility is that severe depression erodes self-control. Another is that chronic emotional pain transforms into anger. Still another is that depression changes how people interpret social situations. Neutral events begin to feel rejecting, humiliating, or threatening. A minor disagreement becomes proof of betrayal. A disappointing interaction becomes evidence that nothing matters anymore.

The law evaluates behavior.

This has important implications for mental health care. When clinicians assess depression, they routinely evaluate suicide risk. Perhaps we should also become more attentive to another question: "Has this person's depression begun to alter how they respond to interpersonal conflict?"

That question is not about predicting crime.

In my own work, I have argued that depression is not merely an episode of sadness but a disorder that can become progressively more complex over time—through chronicity, suicidality, medical illness, psychiatric comorbidity, and perhaps, in some individuals, legal difficulties as well.

If this emerging perspective proves correct, forensic depression will represent something larger than a new research topic. It will remind us that mental disorders do not remain confined within the boundaries of the mind. They ripple outward—into families, workplaces, hospitals, communities, and, occasionally, courtrooms.

Understanding those ripples may ultimately help us prevent them.
